record.title: CLINICOPATHOLOGICAL EVALUATION AND MOLECULAR DETECTION OF HAEMOPARASITES IN SEVERELY ANAEMIC DOGS REFERRED FOR EMERGENCY BLOOD TRANSFUSION
record.abstract: Anaemia in dogs is frequently associated with vector-borne haemoparasitic infections and may progress to a lifethreatening condition requiring emergency blood transfusion.This study investigated the clinicopathological proÞ le of severely anaemic dogs (VPRC <15%) referred for emergency blood transfusion, with emphasis on the molecular detection of haemoparasites and assessment of transfusion compatibility.Anaemic recipient dogs (n = 13) were evaluated using haematology, saline agglutination test (SAT), red blood cell osmotic fragility test, and transfusion compatibility test, and the Þ ndings were compared with those of apparently healthy donor dogs recruited for the study (n = 13).For detection of parasitic aetiology, peripheral blood smear and buffy coat smear examinations, modiÞ ed Knott's test, a PCR panel targeting haemoparasite genera (Babesia spp., Trypanosoma spp., Hepatozoon spp., Anaplasma/Ehrlichia spp., and haemotropic Mycoplasma spp.), and faecal smear examination were performed.Samples positive for haemoparasites at the genus level were subjected to species-level identiÞ cation.The haemoparasites detected in severely anaemic dogs were predominantly B. gibsoni (n = 12; 92.31%), followed by A. platys (n = 1; 7.69%).Molecular detection demonstrated greater sensitivity than conventional microscopy-based methods, with sensitivities of 100% and 66.67%, respectively.Recipients showed marked anaemia and thrombocytopaenia, with severe thrombocytopaenia observed in the A. platys-infected dog.MicroÞ lariae were detected more frequently in peripheral blood smears than by other tests performed on venous blood, suggesting greater detectability of microÞ lariae in peripheral capillary blood.SAT positivity was restricted to cases co-infected with microÞ lariae and B. gibsoni, suggesting a possible association between microÞ lariosis and erythrocyte agglutination.No incompatibilities were detected on cross-matching, consistent with the transfusion-naïve status of the recipient dogs.The Þ ndings highlight the importance of integrating molecular screening of both donors and recipients with conventional parasitological examination for sensitive detection of haemoparasites and compatibility testing to ensure safe blood transfusion practices in endemic regions.

screening.rationale: Clinicopathology of severely anaemic dogs, mostly B. gibsoni, with erythrocyte osmotic fragility and agglutination assessment informing anaemia mechanisms; small cohort, borderline.
